Not to mention that in addition to direct use, there's the issue of groundwater contamination from current farming practices. If I can hijack your comment to go on a semi-tangential rant, the arid landscape in places like CA makes sustainable crop production extremely challenging (especially given the size of CA's agriculture industry, agricultural products being the state's third-largest export category at ~$20bn/year) not only because of water scarcity, but also due to limited nutrient availability. Because of this, use of fertilizers (especially nitrogen-based) has become an integral part of the industry’s viability. The corollary of this is groundwater contamination: a full 96% of CA's nitrate contamination originates with agricultural production (Holbrook 2012).

According to a recent study by the California State Water Resources Control Board (CSWRC), nitrate is a principal contaminant of California groundwater, second only to arsenic; unsafe levels of nitrates were detected in 452 wells in more than 200 communities between 2002 and 2010, representing nearly 6% of all wells sampled over the course of the study (p. 38).

Nitrate-contaminated drinking water is strongly associated with a number of severe medical issues, including thyroid cancer, skin rashes, hair loss, and birth defects, as well as potentially-fatal blood disorder that primarily affects infants (Holbrook). Some emerging research suggests that by 2050, more than 7 in 10 residents of Tulare Lake Basin and Salinas Valley could be at risk of health and financial problems directly attributable to nitrate contamination (more than 2.5 million people live in these areas today) (Ibid.). See also Sarancino & Phipps (2008, p. 76):

Many groundwater contaminants cause harm only after relatively long exposure... Not so for nitrate. Consuming water containing high concentrations of nitrate can have almost immediate effects on a person... Nitrate is very soluble in water and not readily adsorbed by soil, so it is typically very mobile in the subsurface environment.

For the time being, the burden of protecting individuals from nitrate contamination is placed on some of the poorest and most vulnerable communities in California, as well as on budget-conscious providers of public services. Attempting to treat the water supply for groundwater-reliant communities—a default response—unfairly burdens impacted individuals, allowing agricultural firms to externalize these costs in order to maximize their profits. Holbrook article again:

In addition to health risks, tainted water will exact a growing financial toll... Researchers project that utilities and citizens in [Tulare Lake Basin and Salinas Valley] will pay $20 million to $36 million per year for water treatment and alternative supplies for the next 20 years or more.

Note that there is no conditional qualifier attached to this forecast. It doesn't say, “Tainted water will exact a growing financial toll if agricultural policy is not modified,” or “if nitrogen-based fertilizers are not subjected to rigid controls.” The cost projection presented above is independent of any regulatory or behavioral measures we take now; whatever steps are taken to address this issue will almost certainly only impact long-term outcomes; the near-to-medium-term trajectory of nitrate contamination has already been established by past behavior. Plus, small communities will really struggle (and probably be unable) to keep treating water, because high fixed costs disproportionately impact small systems (Harter et al. 2012, p. 2)

Nitrate problems will likely worsen for several decades. For more than half a century, nitrate from fertilizer and animal waste have infiltrated into Tulare Lake Basin and Salinas Valley aquifers. Most nitrate in drinking water wells today was applied to the surface decades ago (Ibid.).

Even so, the use of chemical fertilizers that produce nitrates is on the rise--plus increases "in the production of animals—and animal wastes—has resulted in greater quantities of nitrate leaching into and degrading groundwater.” (Sarancino & Phipps 2008, p. 5).

The problem (in my opinion) isn't carelessness, it's systemic--a function of perverse economic incentives emerging (n part) from poorly-structured regulatory frameworks that not only allow agribusiness to externalize the costs of groundwater contamination directly resulting from their activities, but actually creating a playing field in which that's a requirement for remaining competitive. There are some maybe-OK, kinda-encouraging technical and regulatory solutions folks are working on, but no silver bullets, and the agricultural lobby doesn't make it easy to implement new regulatory constraints, even if they'd very likely be better for everyone (including the companies themselves) in the long run.

I didn't mean to suggest that the answer would be getting rid of the agricultural industry, taking direct measures intended to dial it back, or even to explicitly dial back fertilizer use (which is necessary to maintain crop yields capable of meeting existing demand). Speaking specifically to the groundwater contamination aspect of the issue, a more reasonable approach IMO would be to limit the extent to which agribusiness can externalize some of those environmental/resource/public health costs.

For instance, "pump-and-fertilize" methods (in which agricultural wells are used to recycle water that has already been contaminated with nitrates) seem promising, but they come at a (modest) cost, and there's currently no meaningful market incentive encouraging companies to shoulder the cost of implementing that kind of program. Rather than funding research into new methods of addressing the problem of nitrate contamination using public funds, and rather than subsidizing—even incompletely— the cost of ongoing water treatment in affected communities, I think it would be a smart move on the part of the state and federal governments to implement new regulatory provisions designed to create market incentives encouraging agricultural companies to address these issues themselves. This study looks at how we might go about that (e.g. imposing an input tax on business whose operations contribute to ongoing contamination and using the revenue to do things like subsidize water treatment in at-risk communities, or maybe offer tax breaks to support the implementation of mitigation/monitoring measures, etc.).

I don't think farmers want to fuck up the groundwater, but it's a competitive industry with high demand, and it doesn't make much sense to ask them to voluntarily increase their operating costs--anybody who does is going to be competing with businesses doing shit more affordably.
